claims.text: Adding a minor fraction of an element with a large atomic-size mismatch, such as zirconium, will improve the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
The same addition will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
Zirconium is an example of an added element having a large atomic-size mismatch with the unspecified baseline alloy.
The intervention should be applied during melt synthesis.
The intervention is expected to work under rapid-solidification conditions and an inert atmosphere.
The baseline composition should be near its critical threshold for glass formation for the intervention to be effective.
The beneficial effect will occur only within a limited concentration window of the added element.
The addition will alter short-range atomic order by increasing packing frustration.
The addition will increase local chemical heterogeneity.
Atomic-size mismatch from the added element will induce local strain and disorder.
The induced local strain and disorder will raise the kinetic barrier to crystallization and thereby hinder atomic rearrangement.
The modified alloy will have a higher critical casting thickness than an otherwise identically processed undoped baseline.
The modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the undoped baseline.
Exceeding the beneficial concentration window may cause phase separation or formation of intermetallic compounds.
